title: Sleep and Health
objective: After this level you can explain why sleep matters for health.
summary: CDC advice (from AASM): 9 to 12 hours of sleep at ages 6 to 12, 8 to 10 for teens, 7+ for adults. Sleep helps memory, growth, immunity and the heart.

cards.headline: Only about 1 in 4 US high schoolers gets 8 hours of sleep on a school night.
cards.body: That's from the CDC's 2025 youth survey: 24 percent. How much sleep do experts recommend, and what is the body doing with it?

cards.headline: Where the day gets filed
cards.body: These numbers come from sleep scientists at the American Academy of Sleep Medicine, and they're not about laziness. The NIH says sleep helps you learn and form long-term memories, and in children and teens it supports growth and development. Short on sleep, people struggle to focus and think clearly. So an all-nighter before a test trades away the very thing that helps the studying stick.

cards.headline: A lighter shift for your heart
cards.body: The rest of the body cashes in too. During non-REM sleep your heart rate and blood pressure fall, so your heart doesn't work as hard. Some immune cells work harder while you sleep, and people who don't get enough may catch colds and other infections more easily. The CDC links enough sleep to lower risk of type 2 diabetes, heart disease, high blood pressure and stroke. Sleep is maintenance with the lights off.

questions.prompt: According to the CDC's sleep recommendations, how much sleep do teens aged 13 to 17 need per 24 hours?
questions.explanation: The CDC, following the American Academy of Sleep Medicine, recommends 8 to 10 hours for teens.

questions.prompt: Why can pulling an all-nighter before a test backfire, according to the NIH's sleep research?

options.label: Sleep makes the heart beat faster
options.rationale: Heart rate falls in non-REM sleep.

options.label: Tests are always easier in the morning
options.rationale: The level made no claim about test timing.

options.label: Sleep only matters for adults
options.rationale: Sleep also supports growth in children and teens.

questions.explanation: Sleep helps with learning and forming long-term memories, and too little makes it hard to focus.

questions.prompt: From Level 29: the AHA's heart-health list includes both activity and sleep. Which risk do the CDC and WHO say both of them lower?

options.label: Scurvy
options.rationale: Scurvy comes from too little vitamin C.

options.label: Color blindness
options.rationale: It comes from genes on the X chromosome.

options.label: Altitude sickness
options.rationale: That comes from low air pressure up high.

questions.explanation: Being active and getting healthy sleep are both on the AHA's list, and both are linked to lower risk of high blood pressure.
